W. Murnau]]
[[Albin Grau]]
[[Henrik Galeen]] | portrayer = {{ubl|[[Max Schreck]] ([[Nosferatu|1922]])|[[Klaus Kinski]] ([[Nosferatu the Vampyre|1979]] & [[Vampire in Venice|1988]])|[[Christopher Heyerdahl]] (''[[Are You Afraid of the Dark?]]'')|[[Willem Dafoe]] ([[Shadow of the Vampire|2000]])|Alexander Ward (''[[SpongeBob SquarePants]]'')|[[Doug Jones (actor)|Doug Jones]] ([[Nosferatu (2023 film)|2023]])|[[Bill Skarsgård]] ([[Nosferatu (2024 film)|2024]])}} | voice = | nickname = | alias = {{ubl|[[Count Dracula]]|The Bird of Death|Nosferatu}} | species = [[Vampire]] | gender = Male | nationality = [[Romanians|Romanian]] | based_on = [[Count Dracula]] by [[Bram Stoker]] }} '''Count Orlok''',{{notetag|{{langx|de|Graf Orlok}}; {{langx|ro|Contele Orlok}}; {{langx|hu|Orlok gróf}}}} also known colloquially as '''Nosferatu''', is a fictional character who first appeared in the [[silent film]] ''[[Nosferatu]]'' (1922) directed by [[F. W. Murnau]]. Based on [[Count Dracula]] from [[Bram Stoker]]'s ''[[Dracula]]'', he is played by German actor [[Max Schreck]], and is depicted as a repulsive [[vampire]] descended from [[Belial]], who leaves his homeland of [[Transylvania]] to spread the [[Plague (disease)|plague]] in the idyllic city of Wisborg in [[Biedermeier]]-period Germany, only to find death at the hands of a self-sacrificing woman. Count Orlok would reappear in remakes, played by [[Klaus Kinski]], [[Doug Jones (actor)|Doug Jones]] and [[Bill Skarsgård]], as well as in comic book adaptations and sequels. Orlok's distinct appearance, which is closer to that of [[Vampire folklore by region|vampires of Eastern European folklore]] than to traditional depictions of Dracula, influenced numerous later vampire designs, including those of ''[[Salem's Lot (1979 miniseries)|Salem's Lot]]'', ''[[Buffy the Vampire Slayer]]'' and the ''[[Blade (franchise)|Blade]]'' film franchise, typically in order to distance the creatures from their more conventionally humanized or charming counterparts. ==Name== As ''Nosferatu'' is an unauthorized and unofficial adaptation of [[Bram Stoker]]'s 1897 novel ''[[Dracula]]'', character names were changed in an attempt to avoid accusations of copyright infringement, including changing [[Count Dracula]]'s name to Count Orlok which, according to historian [[Matei Cazacu]], derives from the [[Romanian language|Romanian]] ''[[Vrykolakas|vârcolac]]'',{{Harvnb|Cazacu|2017|p=390}} while [[David Annwn Jones]] links it phonetically to the [[Hungarian language|Hungarian]] ''[[ordog]]''. Jones also notes how ''orlok'' is an archaic form of the [[Dutch language|Dutch]] ''oorlog'', meaning "war".{{Harvnb|Annwn Jones|2023|p=171}} Alternative spellings have included "Orlock", "Orlac" and "Orloc".{{Harvnb|Melton|1999|p=507}} The character is nevertheless referred to as "[[Nosferatu (word)|Nosferatu]]" in the film's publicity material and in director [[F. W. Murnau]]'s annotated copy of the script.{{Harvnb|Eisner|1973|pages=108, 247}} The character is referred to as Dracula in some rereleases of the film.{{Harvnb|Joslin|2017|p=10}} In [[Werner Herzog]]'s 1979 remake, ''[[Nosferatu the Vampyre]]'', the character names revert to those used in the original novel,{{Harvnb|Prager|2012|p=105}} while the [[Nosferatu (2023 film)|2023]] and [[Nosferatu (2024 film)|2024 remakes]] maintain the names used in the original 1922 film. In the 1988 sequel to the 1979 film, ''[[Vampire in Venice]]'', the character is referred to as "Nosferatu". ==Creation== {{multiple image | perrow = | image1 = The Golem , page 2 from the book Der Golem , illustrated by Hugo Steiner-Prag (cropped).jpg | image2 = "The appearance of the Golem", page 6 from the book "Der Golem", illustrated by Hugo Steiner-Prag (cropped).jpg | footer = Illustrations from [[Gustav Meyrink]]'s ''[[The Golem (Meyrink novel)|The Golem]]'', which influenced Orlok's design | direction = horizontal | total_width = 300 | align = right }} The character was largely conceived by Prana Film founder and occultist artist [[Albin Grau]]. Grau claimed he was inspired to shoot ''Nosferatu'' after meeting a farmer during the [[Serbian campaign]], who stated that his father had been a vampire.{{citation |first=Christiane |last=Mückenberger |editor1-first=Günther |editor1-last=Dahlke |editor2-first=Günter |editor2-last=Karl |chapter=Nosferatu |title=Deutsche Spielfilme von den Anfängen bis 1933 |publisher=Henschel Verlag |location=Berlin |date=1993 |isbn=3-89487-009-5 |page=71 |language=de}}{{Harvnb|Annwn Jones|2023|p=174}}{{cite web |url=https://alexanderandsonsrestorations.com/vampires-great-war/ |title=Of Vampires and the Great War |website=alexandersonsrestorations.com|date=30 October 2014 |access-date=2 January 2024 |archive-date=12 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231212104436/https://alexanderandsonsrestorations.com/vampires-great-war/ |url-status=dead }} Grau had a strong influence on Orlok's look, which was inspired by [[Hugo Steiner-Prag]]'s illustrations for [[Gustav Meyrink]]'s ''[[The Golem (Meyrink novel)|The Golem]]''.{{cite AV media | people=Berriatúa, Luciano (director) | year=2007 | title=The Language of Shadows: Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau and His Films | type=documentary | location=Germany | publisher=Friedrich-Wilhelm-Murnau-Stiftung}}{{Harvnb|Giesen|2019|p=18}} He may have also been influenced by the corpses he saw in the trenches of the [[First World War]].{{better source needed|date=June 2025}} Further links to the war have been noticed in Orlok's association with rats, which were a persistent nuisance in the trenches,{{Harvnb|Annwn Jones|2023|p=183}} and the character suddenly appearing enveloped in thick smoke, which has been linked to the poison gas used during the conflict.{{better source needed|date=June 2025}} The character was played by [[Max Schreck]], whose military experiences during the First World War have been thought to have influenced his performance.{{better source needed|date=June 2025}} According to Grau's diary entries, Schreck, when in full makeup, was "shunned" by the Slovak assistants on set. ==Characterization== In ''[[Nosferatu]]'', the Count is described in the fictional book ''Of Vampyres, Ghastly Spirits, Witchcraft, and the Seven Deadly Sins'' as a [[Hematophagy|hematophagous]] creature that dwells in dank caves, tombs and coffins filled with soil gathered from graveyards containing the victims of the [[Black Death]]. The book elaborates that Orlok originated from the "seed of [[Belial]]", an entity described in the [[Dead Sea Scrolls]] as one of four Satanic [[archdemon]]s and associated with pestilence in [[Psalm 41]]: 8-10. [[David Annwn Jones]] notes that this is in contrast to [[Count Dracula]], upon whom the character was based, as Orlok is never stated to have once been human or of being an undead revenant, being instead a creature of demonic lineage who sleeps in coffins merely for the sake of protection against sunlight and convenience in transporting the rats under his command.{{Harvnb|Annwn Jones|2023|pp=169–170}} The film contains no references to a Dracula-like noble ancestry and does not feature any [[Brides of Dracula|brides]] or Roma henchmen, with Orlok's lust for the character of Ellen Hutter being his only human affiliation. Jones further comments that: {{cquote|Though invisibility and partial invisibility and, presumably, the ability to communicate with and transform into animals are shared, other of Dracula's aspects of magic are jettisoned in favour of [[Enochian magic|Enochian]] script and spells. ... In all but the active consumption of blood, Orlok ... [is] closer to the devilish entities in [[Roman Polanski]]'s ''[[Rosemary's Baby (film)|Rosemary's Baby]]'' (1968), [[William Friedkin]]'s ''[[The Exorcist]]'' (1973) and [[Richard Donner]]'s ''[[The Omen]]'' (1976) than to Stoker's vampire.{{Harvnb|Annwn Jones|2023|pp=172–173}}}} As noted by [[J. Gordon Melton]], Orlok resembles folkloric vampires more than Dracula,{{Harvnb|Melton|1999|p=508}} being thoroughly repulsive, sporting a bald head, a beaklike nose, hollowed-out eyes, pointed ears, and sharp fingernails.{{Harvnb|Kinnard|1995|pp=134–138}}{{Harvnb|Kaes|2009|p=105}} His fangs, rather than being elongated [[Canine tooth|canines]], are positioned at the front of his mouth like those of a rat.{{Harvnb|Melton|1999|p=497}} He walks with a slow and labored gait, and his attire consists of a long black coat and tight pants which, according to {{ill|Anton Kaes|de|Anton Kaes}}, "give the impression of skeletal limbs tightly wrapped in funereal clothes". Orlok also lacks Dracula's suave or charm, acting with unrelenting strangeness, with his initial demeanor toward the character of [[Thomas Hutter]] being that of an old Eastern European aristocrat who has outlived his societal usefulness. All of these traits combined preclude the possibility of him ever being mistaken for a human, thus preventing viewers from identifying with him.{{Harvnb|Kinnard|1995|pp=137–138}} He is the first vampire to have been portrayed as being fatally vulnerable to sunlight, with previous vampire portrayals having shown them being uncomfortable with it, but not mortally susceptible.{{Harvnb|Scivally|2015|p=111}} While never seen [[shapeshifting]] in the film, he is nevertheless shown to be capable of walking through walls, as per Stoker. His association with the [[Plague (disease)|plague]], while absent in Dracula, is consistent with vampiric mythology, as vampires were once blamed for several historical epidemics.{{Harvnb|Joslin|2017|pp=14–15}} Unlike Stoker's Dracula, he casts a shadow and reflects in mirrors.{{Harvnb|Giovannini|1997|p=43}}{{Harvnb|Joslin|2017|p=17}} He corresponds with Knock through letters filled with [[Enochian]], [[Hermetic Qabalah|hermetic]] and [[Alchemy|alchemical]] symbols.{{Harvnb|Churton|2014|p=68}} ==Fictional character biography== Count Orlok is a [[vampire]] from [[Transylvania]] known as the ''Totenvogel'' ("Bird of Death" or "Deathbird") who dwells alone in a vast [[castle]] hidden among the rugged peaks in a lost corner of the [[Carpathian Mountains]]. The castle and its master, forgotten by the world for centuries, are swathed in shadows and exhibit a highly sinister feel due to years of neglect. The local [[peasants]] live in terror of phantoms and [[Werewolf|werewolves]] haunting the region and never venture out after dark. During the [[Biedermeier]] period{{Harvnb|Jackson|2013|p=38}} in 1838, Orlok forms a pact with the housing agent Knock, promising him wealth in exchange for a house in the (fictional) city of Wisborg, Germany. Orlok receives Knock's employee, [[Thomas Hutter]], and almost reveals his true nature after Hutter accidentally cuts his finger, causing the Count to briefly lose control. Orlok then feeds off Hutter after he collapses from shock. When Hutter regains consciousness, Orlok signs the documents to purchase the house and notices a miniature portrait of Hutter's wife, Ellen, remarking that she has a "lovely neck." After Hutter discovers Orlok's vampiric nature, the Count attempts to feed off him again, but is repelled when he [[Telepathy|telepathically]] senses Ellen's distress. The next morning, Orlok is discovered "sleeping" in a filthy coffin filled with earth. Hutter then witnesses Orlok loading a cart with several coffins filled with soil, one of which he then hides in, and they are driven off to be loaded onto the ship ''Empusa'' headed for Wisborg. During his journey through Europe, he kills everyone onboard the ''Empusa'' and spreads the [[plague (disease)|plague]] throughout the continent. Upon his arrival in Wisborg, Orlok infests the city with rats that sleep in his coffins, and countless people fall victim to the plague, forcing the local authorities to declare a [[quarantine]] and provoking [[hysteria]] among the citizens. Ellen learns that the Nosferatu can be vanquished only if a woman pure in heart willingly allows him to feed on her long enough to prevent him from seeking shelter from sunrise. Ellen coaxes Orlok to her room and lies in bed whilst he drinks from her neck. The sun rises, and Orlok is burned away in a cloud of smoke. ==Interpretations== In his ''[[From Caligari to Hitler]]'', [[Siegfried Kracauer]] identified Orlok as a "[[Divine retribution|scourge of God]]" comparable to [[Attila]], noting that it was "highly significant that during this period German imagination, regardless of its starting-point, always gravitated towards such figures — as if under the compulsion of love-hate".{{Harvnb|Kracauer|1966|p=79}} [[Matei Cazacu]] draws a parallel between Orlok's attempt at subjugating Wisborg with the failed imperial ambitions of [[Wilhelm II]], but notes that "the vampire at least had the consolation of experiencing love".{{Harvnb|Cazacu|2017|p=276}} {{ill|Anton Kaes|de|Anton Kaes}} notes how Orlok's thirst for blood represents a love of eternal values rather than the "erratic sphere of commerce" represented by Hutter, which would have resonated with contemporary audiences living in a period of [[inflation]] and multicultural tension. Kaes also draws a link between Orlok and the [[shell shock]]ed veterans returning from the [[Eastern Front (World War I)|Eastern Front]], with Orlok being interpreted as the personification of Thomas Hutter's trauma, intruding into his personal life and competing for the love of Ellen.{{Harvnb|Kaes|2009|p=118}} Some authors have compared Orlok's appearance to [[Stereotypes of Jews|stereotypical caricatures of Jewish people]] from the time in which ''Nosferatu'' was produced. His features have also been compared to those of a rat or a mouse, the former of which Jews were often equated with.{{Harvnb|Giesen|2019|pp=108–109}} [[J. Hoberman]] notes how Orlok's actions in the film evoke "both the [[blood libel]] and the accusation of poisoning wells to spread disease that resulted in widespread pogroms and the near-extermination of Jews throughout the Rhineland in the mid-14th century".{{cite web |last=Hoberman |first=J. |author-link=J. Hoberman |title=The Twinned Evils of 'Nosferatu' |url=https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/arts-letters/articles/nosferatu-hoberman-murnau |website=tabletmag.com |publisher=[[Tablet (magazine)|Tablet]] |access-date=28 January 2025 |date=19 May 2020}} Others have said that perceived associations between Orlok and antisemitic stereotypes are unlikely to have been conscious decisions, citing director [[F. W. Murnau]]'s protectiveness of Jewish cast members and status as a homosexual, which would have made him "presumably more sensitive to the persecution of a subgroup inside the larger German society".{{Harvnb|Magistrale|2005|pp=25–26}}{{Harvnb|Jackson|2013|p=20}} ==Reception== Reception to Orlok, and his perceived "monstrousness" compared to other vampires, has been very positive, with publication [[Vulture Magazine]] declaring, "A defining Dracula movie in all but name, Nosferatu is one of the most important and influential films ever made, thanks in part to Schreck’s terrifying Count Orlok. With his teetering build, bat-shaped ears, and curling nails, Orlok remains a potently unsettling villain a hundred years later."{{cite web |last1=Mattison|first1=Celia |title=Dracula Movies Ranked |url=https://www.vulture.com/article/dracula-movie-performances-ranked.html |website=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]] |publisher= Vox Media, LLC. |access-date=31 January 2025 |archive-date=20 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420212603/https://www.vulture.com/article/dracula-movie-performances-ranked.html |url-status=live }} [[Roger Ebert]] praised Schreck's performance as Orlok, noting that it "avoids most of the theatrical touches that would distract from all the later performances ... The vampire should come across not like a flamboyant actor but like a man suffering from a dread curse."{{cite web |last1=Ebert |first1=Roger |title=Nosferatu |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-nosferatu-1922 |website=rogerebert.com |publisher=Ebert Digital, LLC. |access-date=11 November 2022 |archive-date=18 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210218104654/https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-nosferatu-1922 |url-status=live }} Likewise, [[Kim Newman]] praised the monstrous nature of Orlock, stating, "Schreck's vampire is truly nightmarish, scuttling from shadows like something you'd really like to see back under its rock."{{cite web |last1=Newman|first1=Kim |title=Nosferatu Review |url=https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/nosferatu-review/ |website=[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]] |date=January 2011 |publisher=Bauer Media Group, LLC. |access-date=31 January 2024 |archive-date=10 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240510173047/https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/nosferatu-review/ |url-status=live }} Conversely, [[André Gide]] believed the Orlok character was too overtly monstrous to credibly deceive the other characters.{{Cite book |last=Geduld |first=H..M. |year=1972|title=Authors on Film |publisher=Indiana University Press |location=Bloomington |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/3/oa_edited_volume/chapter/2964739}}. ==Later depictions== ===Kinski's portrayals=== {{Quote box |This vampire is someone millions can identify with. He personifies the mingled sadness and desire of people who want to kill themselves because they can't live without physical and spiritual love.|source=[[Klaus Kinski]]{{cite web |last=Jacobs |first=Diane |title="I Become My Characters" |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1979/10/07/archives/i-become-my-characters-i-become-my-characters.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=13 January 2025 |date=7 October 1979 |archive-date=13 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250113212544/https://www.nytimes.com/1979/10/07/archives/i-become-my-characters-i-become-my-characters.html |url-status=live }}|bgcolor=#c6dbf7 |salign=right |width=40%}} The character was portrayed by [[Klaus Kinski]] in [[Werner Herzog]]'s 1979 remake ''[[Nosferatu the Vampyre]]''. Herzog described this incarnation as "not a monster, but an ambivalent, masterful force of change. When the plague threatens, people throw their property into the streets; they discard their bourgeois trappings. A re‐evaluation of life and its meaning takes place."{{cite web |last=Kennedy |first=Harlan |title=Dracula Is a Bourgeois Nightmare, Says Herzog |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1978/07/30/archives/dracula-is-a-bourgeois-nightmare-says-herzog-bourgeois-nightmare.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=13 January 2025 |date=30 July 1978 |archive-date=13 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250113211951/https://www.nytimes.com/1978/07/30/archives/dracula-is-a-bourgeois-nightmare-says-herzog-bourgeois-nightmare.html |url-status=live }} Kinski described him as "a man without free will. He cannot choose, and he cannot cease to be. He is a kind of incarnation of evil, but he is also a man who is suffering, suffering for love. This makes it so much more dramatic, more double‐edged." [[File:Duesseldorf Filmuseum Nosferatu Kinski ohren.jpg|thumb|Prosthetics used by Klaus Kinski for ''[[Nosferatu the Vampyre]]'' at the Filmmuseum Düsseldorf]] Kinski's make-up was an imitation of Max Schreck's in the 1922 original and was applied by Japanese artist Reiko Kruk. Although Kinski fought with Herzog and others during the making of other films, he got along with Kruk, and the four-hour makeup sessions proceeded without any outbursts from Kinski himself.{{cite web |last=Maxwell |first=Patrick |title=''Nosferatu'' Reawakens: An Evening with Werner Herzog and a New 35mm Print of ''Nosferatu the Vampyre'' |url=https://www.moviemaker.com/nosferatu-reawakens-an-evening-with-werner-herzog-and-a-new-35mm-print-of-nosferatu-the-vampyre/ |work=[[MovieMaker]] |publisher=Movie Maker |access-date=27 January 2025 |date=31 January 2023}} Kinski's portrayal was praised by [[Roger Ebert]], who wrote that there is "nothing pleasant about Herzog's vampire", which was "played totally without ego by Klaus Kinski ... [who] does honor to the seriousness of vampires. ... if they were real, here is how they must look",{{cite web |last=Ebert |first=Roger |title=Nosferatu the Vampyre Movie Review (1979) |url=https://rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-nosferatu-the-vampyre-1979 |work=RogerEbert.com |publisher=Ebert Digital LLC |access-date=3 November 2013 |date=24 October 2011 |archive-date=16 February 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140216091449/http://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-nosferatu-the-vampyre-1979 |url-status=live }} while {{ill|Fabio Giovannini|it|Fabio Giovannini}} describes Kinski's portrayal as "without doubt, the most repugnant vampire in cinematic history".{{Harvnb|Giovannini|1997|p=56}} [[David Annwn Jones]] notes how Kinski's character plays down the demonic aspects of the original Orlok and approaches Dracula more closely, as he mentions his noble lineage and has the ability to create more vampires from his victims.{{Harvnb|Annwn Jones|2023|p=191}} Furthermore, Kinski's vampire does not reflect in mirrors, unlike the original. Simon Bacon, in comparing Kinski's performance to Schreck's, notes: {{cquote|Kinski's Dracula not only builds upon the bestial nature of Schreck's vampire – he is visibly ancient and inhuman – but adds a world weariness and melancholy to his persona in keeping with the introspection of the 1970s [[New German Cinema]] movement. ... While Schreck's movements are rigid and arch, mirroring the gothic architecture that so often surrounds him, Kinski's posture is rounded as if he were constricting from within and his movements are generally slow and pained.{{Harvnb|Bacon|2022|p=81}}}} In the 1988 pseudo-sequel to the 1979 remake, ''[[Vampire in Venice]]'', the vampire, played by Kinski once again, is portrayed as a "[[Byronic hero]]" seeking death by having sex with a virgin woman. The film includes several innovations in the vampire myth, showing the monster as being able to walk around in daylight, cast a reflection in mirrors and is undeterred by crosses.{{Harvnb|Curti|2019|p=169}} Kinski initially refused to shave his head and wear fake fangs for the role, though conceded and wore Orlok's traditional rat-like fangs for several scenes.{{Harvnb|Curti|2019|p=168}} Matthew Edwards stated that "Kinski paints his sadistic vampire with a sneering disgust for those around him",{{Harvnb|Edwards|2016|p=290}} while Roberto Curti stated that Kinski's performance "drowns the film".{{Harvnb|Curti|2019|p=170}} ===The Tale of the Midnight Madness=== Orlok was played by [[Christopher Heyerdahl]] in the 26 June 1993 episode of ''[[Are You Afraid of the Dark?]]'', "The Tale of the Midnight Madness." In the episode, a troubled movie theatre finds renewed success when it begins showing a midnight run of a film titled ''Nosferatu: The Demon Vampire'', which is similar to the 1922 film. Things are going well until Orlok steps through the screen into the real world and begins terrorizing the theatre. ''[[SlashFilm]]'' describes Heyerdahl's portrayal as "pretty disturbing" and says that he is "eminently icky as the fabled vampire."{{cite web |last=Spiegel |first=Josh |title=Every Actor Who Has Played Nosferatu (And What They Look Like Without Makeup)|url=https://www.slashfilm.com/1741985/every-actor-played-nosferatu-without-makeup/ |publisher=SlashFilm |access-date=18 May 2025 |date=27 December 2024 }} ===2023 remake=== Orlok was played by [[Doug Jones (actor)|Doug Jones]] in the [[Nosferatu (2023 film)|2023 remake]]. In an interview with ''[[Dread Central]]'', he stated: "I don't think Orlok realizes how much he's faded. In his mind, he's still the dashing count he once was, and that dichotomy fascinated me". His makeup was restricted to his face and hands, and took four hours to apply. Regarding his portrayal, Jones said: "The farther you get from human, the harder it is to play, ... Orlok's humanity is still there, buried under layers of torment and hunger. That's where the real performance comes from—his desires, regrets, and fears".{{cite web |last=Korngut |first=Josh |title=Doug Jones Like You've Never Seen Him Before in 'Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror' |url=https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/519443/doug-jones-like-youve-never-seen-him-before-in-nosferatu-a-symphony-of-horror-january-cover-story/ |work=Dreadcentral.com |publisher=Dread Central |access-date=13 January 2025 |date=9 January 2025 |archive-date=13 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250113214222/https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/519443/doug-jones-like-youve-never-seen-him-before-in-nosferatu-a-symphony-of-horror-january-cover-story/ |url-status=live }} Director David Lee Fisher explained that this interpretation of Orlok was deliberately distanced from Kinski's portrayal and approached Shreck's original performance more closely, being "an elemental force of nature ... definitely destructive, but not necessarily evil".{{cite web |last=Allen |first=Minoo |title=Nosferatu Remixed – An Interview with Director David Lee Fisher |url=https://www.classicmoviehub.com/blog/nosferatu-remixed-an-interview-with-director-david-lee-fisher/ |work=Classicmoviehub.com |publisher=Classic Movie Hub Blog |access-date=27 January 2025 |date=25 November 2014 |archive-date=9 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141209212902/https://www.classicmoviehub.com/blog/nosferatu-remixed-an-interview-with-director-david-lee-fisher/ |url-status=live }} Jones' performance received mixed responses, with Tarryn Gaherty of ''[[Valnet#Collider|Collider]]'' praising him as one of the best aspects of the film, "masterfully combin[ing] physical acting with prosthetics and practical effects",{{cite web |last=Gaherty |first=Tarryn |title=Robert Eggers' 'Nosferatu' Isn't the Only Remake of the Horror Classic Released in 2024 |url=https://collider.com/nosferatu-2024-doug-jones-david-lee-fisher/ |work=Collider.com |publisher=Collider |access-date=27 January 2025 |date=27 December 2024}} while Jennie Kermode of ''Eye For Film'' compared him unfavourably to prior Orlok performers, stating "he cannot capture the same air of uncanny charisma [as Max Schreck], which the film really depends on; neither can he compel the viewer's attention as Klaus Kinski did in his attempts".{{cite web |last=Kermode |first=Jennie |title=Nosferatu |url=https://www.eyeforfilm.co.uk/review/nosferatu-2023-film-review-by-jennie-kermode |work=Eyeforfilm.co.uk |publisher=Eye For Film |access-date=27 January 2025 |date=19 October 2024}} ===2024 remake=== [[Bill Skarsgård]] played Orlok in [[Robert Eggers]]' [[Nosferatu (2024 film)|2024 remake]]. This incarnation, a former [[Solomonari|Solomonar]] who had made a pact with [[Satan]] in a bid for immortality,{{cite web |last=Dubiel |first=Bill |title=Count Orlok's Immense Powers In Nosferatu Have Roots In Old Romanian Folklore |url=https://screenrant.com/nosferatu-count-orlok-vampire-solomonari-romanian-folklore-explainer/ |work=[[Screen Rant]] |publisher=Screen Rant |access-date=14 January 2025 |date=3 January 2025 |archive-date=8 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250108125059/https://screenrant.com/nosferatu-count-orlok-vampire-solomonari-romanian-folklore-explainer/ |url-status=live }} is portrayed as having developed an exploitative psychic bond with Ellen Hutter when she was a child, only to torment her in adulthood once she marries [[Thomas Hutter|Thomas]].{{cite web |last=Hemenway |first=Megan |title=Nosferatu's Love Triangle Explained: Who Does Ellen Really Love? |url=https://screenrant.com/nosferatu-love-triangle-ellen-thomas-count-orlok-explainer/ |work=[[Screen Rant]] |publisher=Screen Rant |access-date=18 March 2025 |date=28 December 2024}} Skarsgård was originally set to play Thomas Hutter, but Eggers decided to cast him as Orlok after seeing his performance as [[Pennywise]] in ''[[It Chapter Two]]''. Eggers' intention was to distance his Orlok from conventional cinematic vampires and to draw inspiration from folklore, resulting in a "hulking brute with a booming voice — less vampire, more undead Transylvanian nobleman", while still retaining details recalling Schreck's portrayal, such as fingernails, posture and the shape of the head.{{cite web |last=Salisbury |first=Mark |title=Robert Eggers on taking his time making 'Nosferatu' and changing Bill Skarsgard's role |url=https://www.screendaily.com/features/robert-eggers-on-taking-his-time-making-nosferatu-and-changing-bill-skarsgards-role/5200552.article |work=Screendaily.com |publisher=Screen Daily |access-date=13 January 2025 |date=9 January 2025 |archive-date=12 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250112104331/https://www.screendaily.com/features/robert-eggers-on-taking-his-time-making-nosferatu-and-changing-bill-skarsgards-role/5200552.article |url-status=live }} The makeup was applied by David White, who modeled the skin tone on that of a 17th-18th century [[wax sculpture]].{{cite web |last=Rawles |first=Timothy |title=iHorror Interviews 'Nosferatu's' Make Up Master David White |url=https://ihorror.com/ihorror-interviews-nosferatus-make-up-master-david-white/ |work=ihorror.com |publisher=iHorror |access-date=27 January 2025 |date=21 January 2025 }} Orlok's design in this film is partially inspired by [[Vlad Dracula]], whom the original Dracula was named after,{{cite web |access-date=3 December 2024 |date=2 December 2024 |first=Damon |last=Wise |title=''Nosferatu'' Review: Robert Eggers' Gothic Romance Is A Perverse, Technically Brilliant Tango With Death |url=https://deadline.com/2024/12/nosferatu-review-robert-eggers-lily-rose-depp-nicholas-hoult-gothic-vampire-romance-1236191438/ |website=[[Deadline Hollywood|Deadline]] |archive-date=3 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203022045/https://deadline.com/2024/12/nosferatu-review-robert-eggers-lily-rose-depp-nicholas-hoult-gothic-vampire-romance-1236191438/ |url-status=live }} with Eggers stating that "there's never been a version of Dracula or [[Nosferatu (word)|Nosferatu]] dressed like a Transylvanian nobleman with authentic [[Transylvanian Hungarians|Hungarian]] attire from the 16th century." Costume designer [[Linda Muir]] sought inspiration from the Transylvanian military from around 1560 to the mid-1600s, incorporating pieces of clothing such as [[dolman]], [[wiktionary:mente#Noun 4|mente]] fur coat, or [[Kalpak|kolpak]] into Orlok's costume.{{Cite web|url=https://i-d.co/article/nosferatu-robert-eggers-making-of-moodboards-costumes/|title=Making Nosferatu Sounds Even More Cursed Than Watching It|date=2024-12-27|access-date=2025-01-15|website=[[i-D]]|last=Greenwood|first=Douglas}} Skarsgård, having refused to have his voice digitally modulated, was trained to lower his voice by Icelandic opera singer [[Ásgerður Júníusdóttir]], incorporating [[Tuvan throat singing|Mongolian throat singing]] into his lines.{{cite web |last=Truitt |first=Brian |title='Nosferatu' star Bill Skarsgård embraced opera to get his vampire voice right |url=https://eu.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/movies/2024/12/30/bill-skarsgard-nosferatu-vampire/77158565007/ |work=[[USA Today]] |publisher=USA Today |access-date=13 January 2025 |date=30 December 2024 |archive-date=13 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250113121939/https://eu.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/movies/2024/12/30/bill-skarsgard-nosferatu-vampire/77158565007/ |url-status=live }} Inspired by Orlok being an ancient Romanian count, Eggers decided to have him speak a reconstructed form of the [[Dacian language]] in the film.{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xl1UKp5K_A0 |title=Making Of NOSFERATU (2024) - Best Of Behind The Scenes, Sets & Talk With Lily-Rose Depp & N. Hoult |date=2024-12-21 |last=STREAM WARS |time=11:31 |access-date=2024-12-29 |quote="When he's doing his spells he speaks ancient Dacian, which is a dead language, and the Dacians were most likely the people who became the ethnic Romanians in Romania." |via=YouTube |archive-date=2024-12-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241227152912/https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=2rlSBTlSNuW7uoii&v=xl1UKp5K_A0&feature=youtu.be |url-status=live }} In creating the interior of Orlok's castle, production designer [[Craig Lathrop]] sought to give it a haunted look by keeping furniture to a minimum. [[Corvin Castle]] was selected for exterior shots for being "in terrible shape", thus coinciding with the "diseased" aesthetic Lathrop wanted. For Orlok's sarcophagus, he incorporated Solomonic sigils and [[Dacians|Dacian]] designs.{{cite web |last=Spratley |first=Leyla |title=Blood, Sweat and Tears |url=https://www.worldofinteriors.com/story/nosferatu-craig-lathrop-horror-interiors-design |work=worldofinteriors.com |publisher=The World of Interiors |access-date=30 January 2025 |date=18 January 2025 }} For his role as Orlok, Skårsgard wore a prosthetic penis, which was kept and framed by his co-star [[Nicholas Hoult]].{{Cite magazine |last=Travis |first=Emlyn |title=Nicholas Hoult says Robert Eggers gifted him Bill Skarsgård's 'Nosferatu' prosthetic penis |url=https://ew.com/nicholas-hoult-says-robert-eggers-sent-bill-skarsgards-prosthetic-penis-nosferatu-8766051 |access-date=2025-07-06 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |language=en}} Skarsgård's performance has been positively received by critics. [[Peter Bradshaw]] described Skarsgård's portrayal as "opaque and forbiddingly gruesome without being necessarily as scary as could be expected",{{cite web |last=Bradshaw |first=Paul |title=Nosferatu review – Robert Eggers's respectful homage to a vampire horror classic |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2024/dec/02/nosferatu-review-robert-eggers-lily-rose-depp-bill-skarsgard |work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=27 January 2025 |date=2 December 2024 }} while [[Matt Zoller Seitz]] described it as Skarsgård's "best work yet" which is best thought not "as a performance, but a repugnant yet strangely mesmerizing obscenity, excavated from a tomb and placed in front of the camera".{{cite web |last=Seitz |first=Matt Zoller |title=Nosferatu |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/nosferatu |work=Rogerebert.com |publisher=Roger Ebert |access-date=27 January 2025 |date=24 December 2024 }} [[Wesley Morris]] described it as "the grossest-looking, ooziest, most cooked, most rotted, most mustached, least-living Dracula I can recall. ... This 'Nosferatu' dares you to feel seduced and sick over the seduction".{{cite web |last=Morris |first=Wesley |title='Nosferatu' Review: Drac's Back, Sucking Blood and Souls |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/12/25/movies/nosferatu-review.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=27 January 2025 |date=25 December 2024 }} ==Legacy== [[File:KurtBarlow1979.jpg|thumb|[[Kurt Barlow]] in the 1979 miniseries ''[[Salem's Lot (1979 miniseries)|Salem's Lot]]'', which was heavily influenced by Count Orlok's design.]] Orlok's fascination with Hutter's picture of his wife and his emergence from his coffin onboard the ''Empusa'' in a "jack-in-the-box" fashion have been imitated in several subsequent ''Dracula'' adaptations. Orlok's design influenced that of [[Kurt Barlow]] in the 1979 miniseries ''[[Salem's Lot (1979 miniseries)|Salem's Lot]]''.{{cite journal |last=Kelley |first=Bill |title=Salem's Lot |url=https://archive.org/details/salems-lot-cinefantastique-magazine/mode/2up |date=1 January 1979 |journal=[[Cinefantastique]] |volume=9 |issue=2 |quote=We went back to the old German ''Nosferatu'' concept where he is the essence of evil, and not anything romantic or smarmy, or, you know, the rouge-cheeked, widow-peaked Dracula. I wanted nothing suave or sexual, because I just didn't think it'd work; we've seen too much of it.}} Orlok-like vampires have also appeared alongside their more conventional counterparts in ''[[Buffy the Vampire Slayer]]'' and the ''[[Blade (franchise)|Blade]]'' film franchise, where they are, according to Simon Bacon, "utilised in order to convey a formidable antagonist in contrast to the increasingly humanised vampires that surround both Buffy and Blade; a return to the monstrosity that underpins the mythology".{{Harvnb|Bacon|2022|p=84}} Orlok's design was also the inspiration behind some non-vampiric creatures, including the [[List of Star Trek aliens#Reman|Reman]]s from ''[[Star Trek: Nemesis]]''{{cite magazine|last=Spelling|first=Ian|date=October 2003|title=Westmore the Merrier|magazine=[[Star Trek Monthly]]|issue= 109|page=32|quote=Stuart [Baird] handed me a picture of Nosferatu and said that was exactly what he wanted. He said, 'I need an alien [species] that looks like this.' And that's exactly what we did. I did some sketches for him and then we went to town on it. We designed the head and ears.}} and the [[Indoraptor]] from ''[[Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom]]''.{{cite web |last=Bui |first=Hoai-Tran |title=Exclusive: 'Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom' Blu-ray Clip Shows How the VFX Team Built the Indoraptor |url=https://www.slashfilm.com/jurassic-world-fallen-kingdom-blu-ray-clip/ |website=/Film |access-date=September 21, 2019 |date=September 13, 2018 |archive-date=September 21, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190921214118/https://www.slashfilm.com/jurassic-world-fallen-kingdom-blu-ray-clip/ |url-status=live |quote="J.A. [Bayona] started to bring references from Nosferatu," VFX producer Dan Barrow says in the featurette highlighting the visual effects that went into creating dinosaurs. "Very specifically the front teeth and the long claws are definitely referencing the Nosferatu character."}} Orlok appeared in the four-part ''[[Nosferatu: Plague of Terror]]'' comic book series by [[Mark Ellis (American author)|Mark Ellis]], which fleshes out his backstory and places him in the modern era. In this series, he is portrayed as a Carpathian nobleman from the 11th century who was killed after becoming a vampire and sealed in his castle, only to be unwittingly resurrected by a [[Crusades|crusader]] whom he vampirises. Orlok then causes havoc throughout history, only to be stopped in contemporary [[Brooklyn]].{{Harvnb|Melton|1999|p=510}} Orlok, referred to as "[[List of SpongeBob SquarePants characters#Nosferatu|Nosferatu]]", was included in the 2002 ''[[SpongeBob SquarePants]]'' episode "[[Graveyard Shift (SpongeBob SquarePants)|Graveyard Shift]]". Writer and storyboard director [[Jay Lender]] had initially wanted to create an original character called "Floorboard Harry", but replaced him with Orlok as a tribute to the magazine series ''[[Famous Monsters of Filmland]]'', which he had enjoyed as a child and where he had first seen images of Orlok. According to ''[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]'' writer James Grebey, "it's entirely possible that more people have seen Count Orlok in that episode of ''SpongeBob'' than have seen ''Nosferatu''". '''Optimus Prime''', also known in [[Japan]] as {{Nihongo|'''Convoy'''|コンボイ}}, is a fictional character in [[Hasbro]]'s ''[[Transformers]]'' franchise. Generally depicted as a brave and noble leader, Optimus Prime is the supreme commander of the [[Autobot]]s in their war against the [[Decepticon]]s. In the ''Transformers'' mythology, Optimus Prime is a Cybertronian, a member of an extraterrestrial species of sentient [[shapeshifting]] robots.

Optimus was based on a Japanese toy from the ''[[Diaclone]]'' toyline, and was developed for the American market after [[Hasbro]] representatives visited the 1983 Tokyo Toy Show. He is regarded as a part of [[popular culture]] and one of the most recognisable fictional characters.

== History and conception ==
Optimus Prime is based on "Battle Convoy",<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barder |first=Ollie |title=Optimus Prime Finally Gets The Diaclone Update He Deserves |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/olliebarder/2020/09/30/optimus-prime-finally-gets-the-diaclone-update-he-deserves/ |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=Forbes |language=en |archive-date=2025-11-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251114030656/https://www.forbes.com/sites/olliebarder/2020/09/30/optimus-prime-finally-gets-the-diaclone-update-he-deserves/ |url-status=live }}</ref> a transforming toy truck from the Japanese ''[[Diaclone]]'' line of toys created by [[Takara]]. [[Hasbro]] representatives visited the 1983 Tokyo Toy Show<ref>{{Cite book |last1=McEniry |first1=Matthew J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FrLuCwAAQBAJ&dq=1983+Tokyo+Toy+Show,+Hasbro&pg=PT39 |title=Marvel Comics into Film: Essays on Adaptations Since the 1940s |last2=Peaslee |first2=Robert Moses |last3=Weiner |first3=Robert G. |date=2016-04-05 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-1-4766-2411-2 |language=en}}</ref> and bought the licenses for multiple Takara toys in order to sell them in the US under the ''Transformers'' brand. The original version of the toy included a human pilot, but this was removed for the ''Transformers'' version.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Plunkett |first=Luke |date=2015-02-09 |title=Transformers Commercials So Old They Weren't Even Called Transformers |url=https://kotaku.com/transformers-commercials-so-old-they-werent-even-called-1684567124 |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=Kotaku |language=en-US |archive-date=2025-12-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251207203427/https://kotaku.com/transformers-commercials-so-old-they-werent-even-called-1684567124 |url-status=live }}</ref> The name "Optimus Prime" was created by [[Dennis O'Neil]] for [[The Transformers (Marvel Comics)|the ''Transformers'' comic]] by [[Marvel Comics]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Prefore |first=Charles |date=2020-05-24 |title=How Marvel Comics Helped Create The TRANSFORMERS |url=https://screenrant.com/transformers-created-marvel-comics/ |access-date=2026-07-03 |website=ScreenRant |language=en}}</ref>

Optimus Prime's truck form is said to be based on the 1980 [[Freightliner Group|Freightliner]] FL86 semi-truck.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Trock |first=Daniel |date=2024-09-29 |title=What Kind Of Semi-Truck Was The Original Optimus Prime? |url=https://www.slashgear.com/1674049/optimus-prime-semi-truck-type/ |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=SlashGear |language=en-US}}</ref> The [[Trailer (vehicle)|trailer]] carried by the toy in truck mode is able transform into a combat deck, and within the trailer is a small scout robot named Roller.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Transformers: The Many Looks of Optimus Prime |url=http://uk.stars.ign.com/articles/996/996813p1.html |access-date=2010-10-12 |work=IGN|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090626065846/http://uk.stars.ign.com/articles/996/996813p1.html|archive-date=2009-06-26|url-status=dead}}</ref> In the 1980s animated series ''[[The Transformers (TV series)|The Transformers]]'', Optimus is voiced by [[Peter Cullen]] in English and [[Tesshō Genda]] in Japanese.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Optimus Prime |url=https://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/tv-shows/The-Transformers/Optimus-Prime/ |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=Behind The Voice Actors |language=en-US |archive-date=2020-11-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112195454/https://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/tv-shows/The-Transformers/Optimus-Prime/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Transformers - The Ride at Universal Studios Singapore, 20240206 1247 6415.jpg|200px|thumb|Optimus Prime, as depicted in the [[Transformers (film series)|live-action film series]], outside ''[[Transformers: The Ride]]'' in Singapore]]

Within his chest is a mystical talisman known as the [[Matrix of Leadership]]. This relic is, according to [[Ron Friedman (producer)|Ron Friedman]], "the cybernetic, philosophical, physical and mystical core of Autobot leadership itself – the [[godhead]]". In ''[[The Transformers: The Movie]]'' (1986), Optimus is killed in his final fight with [[Megatron]] and, on his deathbed, passes the Matrix of Leadership on.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Medievalists.net |date=2025-10-02 |title="One Shall Stand, One Shall Fall": Arthurian Legend Meets Transformers: The Movie |url=https://www.medievalists.net/2025/10/arthurian-legend-transformers-the-movie/ |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=Medievalists.net |language=en-US |archive-date=2026-05-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260520041119/https://www.medievalists.net/2025/10/arthurian-legend-transformers-the-movie/ |url-status=live }}</ref> While Hasbro insisted that Optimus permanently die in the film to make way for a new wave of toys, the film faced significant backlash for the choice. Optimus was ultimately revived in the final episode of the series' third season, and has since consistently served as the leader of the Autobots in various other forms of ''Transformers'' media. Plots involving Optimus dying and coming back to life have featured frequently in the franchise.<ref name=":0" />

== Reception ==
Due to the popularity of the ''Transformers'' franchise and Optimus Prime's position as one of its most iconic characters, he is commonly regarded as among the most recognizable fictional characters of all time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pruitt |first=Cenate |date=2024-01-01 |title=Transformational Figure: Optimus Prime in Popular Culture 2006–2018 |url=https://www.academia.edu/122321314 |journal=REDEN. Revista Española de Estudios Norteamericanos|volume=5 |issue=2 |doi=10.37536/reden.2024.5.2358 |doi-access=free |hdl=10017/61950 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> He was named the 30th greatest movie hero of all time by ''[[Total Film Magazine]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2007-11-26 |title=Top heroes and villains named in movie list |url=http://www.news.com.au/goodies-baddies-get-sorted/story-e6frfmq9-1111114966889 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110804010059/http://www.news.com.au/goodies-baddies-get-sorted/story-e6frfmq9-1111114966889 |archive-date=2011-08-04 |access-date=2011-09-23 |publisher=News.com.au}}</ref> In March 2023, Optimus Prime received a Lifetime Achievement Award from the [[Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Blanchet |first=Ben |date=5 March 2023 |title=Optimus Prime Rolls Out To Praise With Unusual Honor At Kids' Choice Awards 2023 |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/optimus-prime-lifetime-achievement-award_n_640452ede4b0586db70e320a |access-date=2023-03-05 |publisher=Huffington Post}}</ref> In May 2026, actress [[Inde Navarrette]] considered Optimus her "celebrity crush" in multiple interviews and social media interactions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Apatoff |first=Alex |date=15 May 2026 |title=Inde Navarrette Is Your New Obsession |url=https://www.interviewmagazine.com/film/inde-navarrette-is-your-new-obsession |access-date=2026-05-23 |publisher=Interview Magazine |archive-date=2026-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260514212141/https://www.interviewmagazine.com/film/inde-navarrette-is-your-new-obsession |url-status=live }}</ref>

A study by historian Scott Manning published in ''[[Studies in Medievalism]]'' argued that Prime's role in ''The Transformers: The Movie'' echoes the themes in [[King Arthur|Arthurian]] mythology. In particular, Manning claimed that the motif of Optimus dying and being reborn echoes the motif of the "once and future king", and that the Matrix of Leadership and its status as the godhead echo medieval representations of the [[Holy Grail]].<ref name=":0" />

'''Art the Clown''' is a fictional character and the primary antagonist in the [[Terrifier (film series)|''Terrifier'' film series]] and related media. Created by [[Damien Leone]], the character first appeared in the short films ''The 9th Circle'' (2008) and ''Terrifier'' (2011). Both shorts were included in the anthology film ''[[All Hallows' Eve (2013 film)|All Hallows' Eve]]'' (2013), which marked the character's feature film debut. In these early appearances, he was portrayed by Mike Giannelli before his retirement from acting. He was replaced by [[David Howard Thornton]], who portrayed Art in ''[[Terrifier]]'' (2016), ''[[Terrifier 2]]'' (2022), and ''[[Terrifier 3]]'' (2024). 

Art debuted as a background character in Leone's directorial debut short film to test out different horror concepts. Audiences responded strongly to Art, leading Leone to develop the character into a recurring [[Slasher film|slasher]] villain over the next decade. Art became a [[pop culture]] figure and iconic [[evil clown]] after the critical and commercial success of ''Terrifier 2''.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://collider.com/terrifier-art-the-clown-horror-icon/|title=Terrifier's Art the Clown Is the Horror Icon of the 2020s|last=Hollman|first=Raquel|work=Collider|access-date=May 14, 2023|date=October 11, 2023|archive-date=May 14, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230514180318/https://collider.com/terrifier-art-the-clown-horror-icon/|url-status=live}}</ref> The character's background remains ambiguous, although all of his appearances show him possessing [[supernatural]] abilities. His archenemy is the [[final girl]] [[Sienna Shaw]] ([[Lauren LaVera]]), with Leone writing Sienna and Art to reflect [[Bible|biblical]] undertones of [[good and evil]].

==Concept and creation==
Leone's idea of Art originated from his concept of a woman getting off work and taking the city bus home, where a clown gets on and sits across from her, taunting her.<ref name="Origins">{{cite web |last1=Bilodeau |first1=Matthew |title=How Terrifier's Art The Clown Was Created |url=https://www.slashfilm.com/1070233/how-terrifiers-art-the-clown-was-created/ |website=[[/Film]] |access-date=17 April 2023 |date=January 20, 2023 |archive-date=2 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240802141452/https://www.slashfilm.com/1070233/how-terrifiers-art-the-clown-was-created/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He envisioned Art as a combination of being uncomfortable and comedic to viewers—but with the character becoming "progressively more intimidating and aggressive."<ref name="Origins" /> Art got incorporated into Leone's directorial debut, the short film "The 9th Circle" (2008), merely as a background character, as Leone states, "I threw in everything, clowns, witches, demons, monsters, everything up against the wall hoping something would stick."<ref name="Origins" />

Art appeared next in Leone's follow-up film, the short film ''Terrifier'' (2011), which followed Art's pursuit of a costume designer that witnessed one of his murders at a gas station; he had a more substantial role in this film after people who viewed "The 9th Circle" expressed interest about him to Leone.<ref name="Origins" /> Film producer Jesse Baget, who saw the short films on [[YouTube]], approached Leone about including them in an [[anthology film]].<ref name="Origins" /> Leone saw this as an opportunity to direct a feature film of Art, and he ultimately agreed.<ref name="Origins" /> It would evolve into ''All Hallows' Eve'' (2013) and included a wraparound story of a babysitter that becomes the target of Art after one of the children she's watching receives a VHS tape depicting Art after [[trick-or-treating]].<ref name="Origins" /> This anthology film would further implicate Art being a supernatural entity, although his background remains ambiguous.<ref name="Origins" /> Actor Mike Giannelli, who is a friend of Leone, portrayed Art in all of these appearances before retiring from acting.<ref name="2016 film">{{cite web |last1=Taylor |first1=Nick |title=Horror Business: The Making of Damien Leone's TERRIFIER |url=https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/277512/horror-business-the-making-of-damien-leones-terrifier/ |website=[[Dread Central]] |access-date=17 April 2023 |date=July 2, 2018 |archive-date=30 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190930215930/https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/277512/horror-business-the-making-of-damien-leones-terrifier/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Terrifier 2 Success">{{cite web |last1=Whittaker |first1=Richard |title=How Art the Clown Became a Horror Icon |url=https://www.austinchronicle.com/screens/2022-09-23/how-art-the-clown-became-a-horror-icon/ |website=[[The Austin Chronicle]] |access-date=18 April 2023 |date=September 23, 2022 |archive-date=2024-09-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240919203157/https://www.austinchronicle.com/screens/2022-09-23/how-art-the-clown-became-a-horror-icon/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:David Howard Thornton (53039363451) (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|[[David Howard Thornton]] first played Art in the feature-length version of ''Terrifier'']]

After the release of ''All Hallows' Eve'', Leone wanted to create a feature-length film focusing solely on Art as he believed the 2010s lacked an iconic horror villain, particularly an original clown character.<ref name="2016 film" /> He aimed to make Art the opposite of [[Pennywise|Pennywise the Dancing Clown]] both in characterization and appearance; Art is bald, does not speak, uses weapons, and wears makeup and clothes devoid of color. However, in contrast to silent killers such as [[Leatherface]], [[Michael Myers (Halloween)|Michael Myers]] and [[Jason Voorhees]], Art is highly expressive and emotional.<ref name="2016 film" /> Following Giannelli's retirement, [[David Howard Thornton]] was cast in the role.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://deadline.com/2023/05/terrifier-sequel-art-clown-release-details-bigger-budget-box-office-hit-1235383506/|title='Terrifier 3': Details Revealed For Bigger Budget Threequel After Second Film's Box Office Breakout|website=[[Deadline Hollywood|Deadline]]|first=Andreas|last=Wiseman|date=May 31, 2023|access-date=May 31, 2023|archive-date=May 31, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230531163744/https://deadline.com/2023/05/terrifier-sequel-art-clown-release-details-bigger-budget-box-office-hit-1235383506/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bloody-disgusting.com/movie/3763948/terrifier-3-is-officially-happening-and-will-continue-to-push-boundaries/|title='Terrifier 3' Is Officially Happening and Will Continue to Push Boundaries!|website=[[Bloody Disgusting]]|first=Brad|last=Miska|date=May 31, 2023|access-date=May 31, 2023|archive-date=May 31, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230531162803/https://bloody-disgusting.com/movie/3763948/terrifier-3-is-officially-happening-and-will-continue-to-push-boundaries/|url-status=live}}</ref> Leone describes the difference in casting as, "Mike may as well have been a guy dressed as a clown, whereas David is a clown. If you know him in person, he is a walking cartoon. He is [[Roger Rabbit]] in real life, and you'd never believe that he's Art the Clown, but he knows how to flip the switch and bring it to a dark place."<ref name="Terrifier 2 Success" /> Thornton saw a posting on the [[digital casting]] website Actors Access for a "tall, skinny, comedic actor that had experience in clowning and comedy".<ref name="Thornton">{{cite web |last1=Boiselle |first1=Matt |title=Interview: David Howard Thornton Steps Into The Big Shoes Of Art The Clown |url=https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/269479/interview-david-howard-thornton-steps-into-the-big-shoes-of-art-the-clown/ |website=[[Dread Central]] |access-date=17 April 2023 |date=March 25, 2018 |archive-date=30 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190930215848/https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/269479/interview-david-howard-thornton-steps-into-the-big-shoes-of-art-the-clown/ |url-status=live }}</ref> As he was familiar with Art the Clown through ''All Hallows' Eve'', Thornton asked his agent to submit him for it; after improvising a kill scene during his audition, he got cast in the role.<ref name="Thornton" />

==Film appearances==
The character made his debut appearance in the short film ''The 9th Circle'' (2008), which follows his pursuit of a young woman named Casey (Kayla Lian) in an empty train station on Halloween night. Merely a supporting character in this film, Art abducts Casey, bringing her to a satanic cult for a sacrifice to [[Satan]].<ref>{{cite video|people=Damien Leone (Director)|title=The 9th Circle|medium=DVD|location=United States|date=2008}}</ref>

Art's second appearance occurred in the short film ''Terrifier'' (2011), where he stalks and torments a young woman who witnesses one of his murders at a gas station.<ref>{{cite video|people=Damien Leone (Director)|title=Terrifier|medium=DVD|location=United States|publisher=D&D Films LLC|date=2011}}</ref> 

The character made his feature-film debut in ''All Hallows' Eve'' (2013)<ref>{{Citation|title=All Hallows' Eve|url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt2900624/|access-date=2020-03-31|archive-date=2024-07-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240711193925/https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2900624/|url-status=live}}</ref> which incorporates the prior two short films as segments on [[VHS]] tapes that the film's protagonist Sarah (Katie Maguire) watches with the children she's babysitting on Halloween night. Art enters the real world and murders the children for a terrified Sarah to find.<ref>{{cite video|people=Damien Leone (Director)|title=All Hallows' Eve|medium=DVD|location=United States|publisher=Ruthless Pictures|date=2013}}</ref>

Art's second feature-film appearance was in the slasher film ''[[Terrifier]]'' (2016). Set on Halloween night in fictitious Miles County, New York, ''Terrifier'' sees Art pursue partygoer Tara Heyes ([[Jenna Kanell]]), her younger sister [[Vicky Heyes|Vicky]] ([[Samantha Scaffidi]]), and her best friend Dawn Emerson ([[Catherine Corcoran]]). After killing Tara and Dawn, Art targets Vicky, the lone survivor. She fights against Art until he runs her over with a [[pickup truck]] and eats half of her face, leaving her disfigured. Before he can kill her, the police confront him at gunpoint; he shoots himself.

In ''[[Terrifier 2]]'' (2022), a sinister entity known as the Little Pale Girl (Amelie McLain) resurrects Art and accompanies him in his pursuit of Sienna Shaw ([[Lauren LaVera]]) and Sienna's younger brother, Jonathan (Elliot Fullam). Their father, Michael ([[Jason Patric]]), was an artist that died from a brain tumor. Having envisioned Art and his victims in his prophetic sketches, Michael drew Sienna as an angel-warrior-attired heroine fated to defeat Art; thus, before his death, Michael also gifted Sienna a sword. Sienna, who made a Halloween costume based on her father's sketches, battles Art in an abandoned [[carnival]]. Art is defeated after Sienna decapitates him with her father's sword. However, he is brought back to life after Vicky Heyes, who is in a mental hospital, gives birth to his living head as his new mother, and is possessed by the Little Pale Girl.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bloody-disgusting.com/movie/3714685/terrifier-2-damien-leone-previews-gruesome-return-of-terrifier-character/|title='Terrifier 2': Damien Leone Previews Gruesome Return of 'Terrifier' 2022|access-date=April 2, 2023|archive-date=April 2, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230402190026/https://collider.com/terrifier-2-ending-explained/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In ''[[Terrifier 3]]'' (2024), Art's headless body reanimates inside the Terrifier carnival and makes its way to Miles County's psychiatric hospital, where Art reattaches his head after helping the possessed Victoria tear apart a security guard. The duo escape to an abandoned mansion, then spend the next five years in hibernation. In December 2023, they reawaken and set off on another killing spree. They track down Sienna and invade her home, killing her aunt, Jessica ([[Margaret Anne Florence]]) and her uncle Greg ([[Bryce Johnson]]) in front of her. The demonic entities add more horror when they reveal an unrecognizable skull that according to them belongs to Jonathan. Fortunately, Sienna fights against the spirit of the Little Pale Girl, preventing it from invading her body, partially because she still has her cousin Gabbie (Antonella Rose) to fight for. Through a clever strategy from Gabbie, Sienna gains control of her sword, using it to kill Victoria and presumably the Little Pale Girl inside her. Art attacks Sienna with his chainsaw but is ultimately pinned to a wall. Vicky's corpse creates a portal to Hell and Sienna sees herself forced to abandon Art to save Gabbie, only for the younger girl to fall into the mysterious realm alongside the sword. Taking advantage of Sienna's distraction, Art escapes through a window and catches a bus, where he honks his horn at a woman as she reads a book called "The 9th Circle."

''Terrifier 4'' is currently in the works and will feature Art's backstory within the first 15 minutes of the film according to Leone.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://movieweb.com/terrifier-4-damien-leone-art-the-clown-backstory-first-15-minutes/|work=Movie Web|title=Creator of 2024's Most Shocking Horror Hit Promises to Finally Give Fans What They Want in "Epic" Sequel|author=Melzer, James|date=May 30, 2025|accessdate=May 30, 2025}}</ref>

==In other media==

==Reception==
In a positive review for the magazine ''[[Starburst (magazine)|Starburst]]'', Sol Harris wrote "Art is a truly enigmatic and memorable villain. He frequently veers into the territory of being genuinely unpleasant to watch, which makes him feel somewhat separate from the stable of horror icons such as [[Freddy Krueger]] and [[Chucky (character)|Chucky]]. Special acknowledgement should be given to David Howard Thornton for a truly wonderful performance and one that easily stands toe-to-toe with the likes of [[Tim Curry|Curry]] and [[Bill Skarsgård|Skarsgård]]."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Harris |first1=Sol |title=TERRIFIER |url=https://www.starburstmagazine.com/reviews/terrifier-2 |website=Starburst |date=28 March 2018 |access-date=31 December 2020 |archive-date=21 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231021180716/https://www.starburstmagazine.com/reviews/terrifier-2/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In a more middling review, the blog [[Film School Rejects]] praised Thornton's portrayal and use of body language but panned ''Terrifier'' and deemed the character a misogynist with "a deep hatred for women".<ref>{{cite web |title='Terrifier' Review: Please Do Not Send In The Clowns |url=https://filmschoolrejects.com/terrifier-review/ |website=Film School Rejects |date=23 October 2019 |access-date=31 December 2020 |archive-date=27 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240827010634/https://filmschoolrejects.com/terrifier-review/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
